title: Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium
keyIdea: A reversible reaction (⇌) can go both ways: reactants form products and products re-form reactants. In a closed system it reaches dynamic equilibrium: the forward and backward reactions keep going at equal rates, so the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant. Constant does not mean equal, and the reactions have not stopped.
familyTip: In a school lab, with eye protection, heat a little blue hydrated copper sulfate until it turns white, let it cool, then add a few drops of water: it turns blue again and gets warm. Ask: is this reaction reversible, and why is the open tube not at equilibrium?

visual.caption: Is each statement true or false for a reaction at dynamic equilibrium? Drag each card, or tap it then a box.

items: Forward and backward rates are equal
Amounts of reactants and products stay constant
Reactant and product amounts must be equal
A product gas escaping keeps it at equilibrium

lab.caption: Flagship lab: run A ⇌ B from all A, find where the rates meet, start from all B, tag one particle, open the flask, change kf and kb.

kid: Some reactions go both ways. We show this with the ⇌ sign. For A ⇌ B, A turns into B, and B can turn back into A.
Start with only A. At first only the forward reaction can happen, so it is fast. As B builds up, the backward reaction speeds up, and as A is used up, the forward one slows down.
Soon the two rates are equal. B is made as fast as it is used up, so the amounts stop changing. This is dynamic equilibrium: both reactions still go on.
It only works in a closed system. If a product escapes, it cannot turn back, so the forward reaction runs until the reactant is used up.
adult: Ages 16 to 18. AQA A-level Chemistry 3.1.6.1 and OCR A 3.2.3: in a reversible reaction at equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions proceed at equal rates and the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant; this needs a closed system. NGSS HS-PS1-6 asks students to refine a system to change the amount of product at equilibrium.

The lab uses A ⇌ B with first-order steps, so the forward rate is kf[A] and the backward rate is kb[B]. Setting them equal gives [B]/[A] = kf/kb, the same mix from either starting side at a fixed temperature. Hydrated copper sulfate losing water when heated in an open tube is reversible but not at equilibrium, because the water escapes.

Common mistakes: saying the reactions stop at equilibrium; thinking equal rates means equal concentrations (or 50:50); thinking the side you start from changes the mix; and forgetting the closed-system condition.

In the lab the learner runs A ⇌ B from all A, drags a time line to where the rates meet, runs from all B, tags one particle to watch it keep swapping, opens the flask so B escapes, and changes kf and kb.

practice.prompt: Why is the equilibrium called dynamic?
choices: Both reactions keep going at equal rates
Both reactions have stopped
The amounts keep changing
practice.hint: Think about the tagged particle in the lab once the totals were steady.
practice.explain: Particles keep reacting both ways, but at equal rates, so the totals stay constant. Dynamic means still moving, not stopped.

practice.prompt: In A ⇌ B, kf is {a} times kb. At equilibrium, what is [B] ÷ [A]?
practice.hint: At equilibrium kf × [A] = kb × [B]. Rearrange for [B]/[A].
practice.explain: kf[A] = kb[B], so [B]/[A] = kf/kb = {a}. A faster forward step leaves more B at equilibrium.

practice.prompt: A closed flask holds {=(a+1)*m} particles of A and B in total. At equilibrium there are {a} B particles for every A particle. How many B particles are there?
practice.hint: Split the total in the ratio B : A = {a} : 1.
practice.explain: There are {=a+1} parts in total, so one part is {m} particles. B has {a} parts: {a} × {m} = {=a*m} particles.

practice.prompt: Starting with only B instead of only A (same temperature, closed flask), the equilibrium mix is …
choices: The same as starting from A
All B
The reverse of starting from A
practice.hint: The mix is fixed by kf × [A] = kb × [B]. Does that depend on the start?
practice.explain: Both runs settle where kf[A] = kb[B], so they reach the same mix. The starting side does not set the position.

practice.prompt: Blue hydrated copper sulfate turns white when heated in an open tube. Why is this not an equilibrium?
choices: The water escapes, so the backward reaction cannot happen
It is not a reversible reaction
Heat stops all reactions
practice.hint: What does dynamic equilibrium need, and where does the steam go?
practice.explain: The reaction is reversible (add water and it turns blue again), but in an open tube the water leaves, so the system is not closed.

pool.prompt: At dynamic equilibrium, which statement is true?
choices: The concentrations stay constant
The concentrations are equal
The reactions have stopped
pool.hint: Constant and equal are not the same thing.
pool.explain: The rates are equal, so the concentrations stop changing. They are usually not equal to each other.

pool.prompt: At equilibrium, A turns into B {a} times per second in a flask. How many times does B turn into A in {b} seconds?
pool.hint: At equilibrium the backward rate equals the forward rate.
pool.explain: The backward rate is also {a} per second, so in {b} seconds there are {a} × {b} = {=a*b} B → A events.

pool.prompt: At equilibrium in A ⇌ B, [B] is {k} times [A]. If kb = {b} s⁻¹, what is kf in s⁻¹?
pool.hint: Use kf × [A] = kb × [B], so kf = kb × [B]/[A].

choices: The reaction can go both forwards and backwards
The reaction has finished
The reactants and products are equal
pool.explain: ⇌ marks a reversible reaction: products can re-form reactants as well as the other way round.

pool.prompt: Start with only A. What happens to the forward rate as time goes on?
choices: It falls, then stays steady
It rises, then stays steady
It stays the same from the start
pool.hint: The forward rate depends on how much A is left.
pool.explain: As A is used up the forward rate falls, while the backward rate rises with B, until the two are equal and steady.

pool.prompt: Jo says the reaction has stopped because the colour no longer changes. What is wrong?
choices: Both reactions continue at equal rates, so the colour stays the same
Nothing: no change means no reaction
The colour only stops changing in an open flask
pool.hint: Steady totals can come from two equal, opposite changes.
pool.explain: At dynamic equilibrium, particles still react both ways at the same rate, so the amounts, and the colour, stay constant.

pool.prompt: In A ⇌ B a product gas B escapes from an open flask. What happens?
choices: The reaction goes on until A is used up
A new equilibrium forms with the same mix
The forward reaction stops at once
pool.hint: Can escaped B turn back into A?
pool.explain: Escaped B cannot react backwards, so the backward rate stays low and A keeps turning into B until it runs out.

pool.prompt: kf = 0.6 s⁻¹ and kb = 0.4 s⁻¹ for A ⇌ B. What percentage is B at equilibrium?
pool.hint: [B]/[A] = kf/kb = 0.6/0.4. Turn the ratio 3 : 2 into a percentage.
pool.explain: [B] : [A] = 0.6 : 0.4 = 3 : 2, so B is 3/5 = 60%. 50% assumes equal amounts; 40% swaps A and B.

pool.prompt: Put these in order for A ⇌ B starting with only A.
items: Some of the new B turns back into A
The rates become equal and the amounts stay constant
pool.hint: What can happen before there is any B?
pool.explain: With only A, nothing can go backwards. Once B forms, some turns back into A; the backward rate rises and the forward rate falls until they are equal: dynamic equilibrium.
